01 · Root finding

Bisection method

f(x) = x² − 25. Start with an interval [a, b] where f changes sign, then repeatedly halve it — keeping whichever half still brackets the root — until it's tiny.

a
b
Iteration log
02 · Root finding

False position method

Same bracket [a, b] as bisection, but instead of the midpoint, draw a straight line between (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) — the root of that line is the next guess.

a
b
Iteration log
03 · Root finding

Newton–Raphson method

f(x) = x² − 25, f′(x) = 2x. From a starting guess, follow the tangent line down to where it crosses zero — that's the next guess. Converges fast when it converges at all.

x₀
Iteration log
04 · Integration

Trapezoidal rule

f(x) = x² on [0, 2], split into 10 strips. Each strip is approximated as a trapezoid; the total area builds up one strip at a time.

Running sum
05 · Integration

Simpson's 1/3 rule

f(x) = x³ on [0, 1], split into 10 strips. Points alternate weight 4 and 2 (endpoints get weight 1) — a weighted sum that's exact for cubics.

Weighted sum

Analytical integration

The baseline every numerical method above is checked against: ∫sin(x)dx from 0 to 1, solved exactly as −cos(b) + cos(a).

Statistical Physics Lab

Nine systems, one idea: order from randomness.

Every simulation in this module pushes random, microscopic events — a spin flip, a step, a collision — and watches what statistical pattern falls out at the large scale. Each topic below follows the same path: the physics behind it, a live run you can watch, and the actual output the code produced.

01 · 1D Ising model 02 · 1D random walk 03 · 2D random walk 04 · Boltzmann distribution 05 · Harmonic oscillators 06 · Molecular dynamics 07 · Monte Carlo estimate of π 08 · Probability distributions
01 · Statistical Physics Lab

The 1D Ising model, from idea to result.

A chain of magnetic spins, simulated with the Metropolis algorithm. This page walks through it the way the code does — first the physics, then a live run, then the actual output from the repository.

Spins on a line

The 1D Ising model represents a chain of N particles, each holding a spin sᵢ that points either up (+1) or down (−1). Neighbouring spins interact — in the ferromagnetic case, they'd rather point the same way, because that lowers the system's energy.

E = −J Σᵢ sᵢ·sᵢ₊₁ − h Σᵢ sᵢ

J is the coupling strength between neighbours and h is an external magnetic field. With J > 0, aligned neighbours (↑↑ or ↓↓) lower the energy; misaligned neighbours (↑↓) raise it.

How the simulation decides

The code doesn't try every configuration — it uses the Metropolis algorithm: pick a random spin, work out how much the energy would change (ΔE) if it flipped, then:

— if ΔE ≤ 0, flip it (the system likes lower energy)
— otherwise, flip it anyway with probability e^(−ΔE / T)

That second rule is what lets the system explore high-energy states occasionally — exactly as much as temperature allows. Run this over many steps and the chain settles into a realistic thermal equilibrium at temperature T.

Expected behaviour: at low T, spins mostly align — thermal noise is too weak to fight the coupling. At high T, thermal fluctuations win, and spins flip freely — the chain looks disordered.
Same chain, two temperatures — this is what "order" and "disorder" look like for a spin chain.
Temperature T = 1.50
Live state — N = 40 spins
steps run0
magnetisation ⟨s⟩—
energy / N—

Drag the temperature slider while it runs. At low T the row should settle into long stretches of one colour; push T up and it turns to static.

These four plots are the actual output of the Python script in the repository — the same Metropolis simulation above, but run properly: averaged over many steps, at 100 temperatures from 0.1 to 10. Here's what each one is showing, and why it looks the way it does.

Average energy vs temperature

Near T = 0, energy sits at −1 per spin — every neighbour pair is aligned, the lowest energy the chain can have. As T rises, thermal flips break bonds one by one, so energy climbs toward 0. The curve is steepest right where the order breaks down fastest.

1D-ising-model.py · output

Average magnetisation vs temperature

Starts at 1 — fully aligned — and drops sharply around T ≈ 0.5–1, then trails off toward a small residual value. That drop is the chain losing long-range order as thermal noise overwhelms the coupling between neighbours.

1D-ising-model.py · output

Specific heat vs temperature

Specific heat measures how much the energy fluctuates — C ∝ Var(E)/T². It peaks exactly where the energy curve is steepest, because that's where a small change in T causes the biggest change in how ordered the chain is.

1D-ising-model.py · output

Magnetic susceptibility vs temperature

Susceptibility measures how much the magnetisation fluctuates — χ ∝ Var(M)/T. Like specific heat, it spikes at the same crossover temperature: the chain is most sensitive to small nudges right where it's deciding between order and disorder.

1D-ising-model.py · output
A technical note worth having, since it's easy to over-read this: a true infinite 1D Ising chain (no field, nearest-neighbour only) has no phase transition at any finite T — order always eventually breaks down. What these plots capture is a finite-size, finite-run crossover: with N = 100 spins and a limited number of Monte Carlo steps, the chain behaves as if it has a "critical" temperature, even though the sharp transition itself is a 2D-and-above phenomenon. That's a real and useful thing to see in simulation — just worth naming correctly if this goes in a report.
02 · From ordered spins to random steps

1D random walk

The Ising model flips one spin at a time by chance. Strip away everything except that one idea — a random choice made over and over — and you get a random walk. Each step, the walker moves left or right with equal probability; the lattice wraps around at ±10, exactly like the code.

i · the physics

A position after N random ±1 steps is a sum of N independent random variables. Its mean stays at 0 by symmetry, but its variance grows linearly with N — that's the signature of diffusion, and it's the same statistical mechanism that produces the mean-square displacement of a diffusing particle, or the drift of a value under repeated random perturbation.

Var(position) ≈ N · Var(one step) = N

With 50 trials per run, the code's own numbers land close to this: a standard deviation of about 5.85, so a variance near 34 — a bit under the naive N = 50 because the periodic wraparound folds large excursions back into the middle.

Same coin-flip logic as Metropolis picking a spin to flip — just without an energy cost attached.

03 · The same idea, one dimension up

2D random walk

Same rule, extra freedom: each step now goes up, down, left, or right with equal probability, on a grid that wraps at ±10 in both directions.

i · the physics

The displacement in x and the displacement in y are each independent 1D random walks. So the mean-square distance from the origin still grows linearly with the number of steps — ⟨r²⟩ ∝ t — just distributed isotropically across a plane instead of a line.

This is the textbook toy model for diffusion: a particle undergoing many uncorrelated random collisions traces exactly this kind of path. It's also the geometric skeleton behind the molecular dynamics simulation later in this module, where particles' actual trajectories look qualitatively similar, driven by real forces instead of coin flips.

Up / down / left / right, picked uniformly at random every step.

04 · The rule underneath everything else here

Boltzmann distribution

This is the formula that decided whether the Ising model's Metropolis step accepted a flip. Here it is on its own: the probability of a system occupying an energy level E, at temperature T.

i · the physics
P(E) = e^(−E / T) / Z,   where Z = Σ e^(−Eᵢ / T)

Z, the partition function, is just a normalising sum over every possible energy level so the probabilities add to 1. The important part is the exponential: low-energy states are always favoured, but how much more favoured depends entirely on temperature.

At low T, e^(−E/T) collapses fast as E grows — the system is overwhelmingly likely to sit in its lowest energy levels. At high T, the exponential decays slowly, so probability spreads out across many energy levels almost evenly. This exact trade-off is what let the Ising model order at low T and randomise at high T.

ii · watch it happen
Temperature T = 200
Reading the curve

energy at which P drops to half—

Slide temperature up and watch the curve flatten and stretch — exactly the low-T-orders, high-T-randomises trade-off from the Ising model, isolated from everything else.

iii · the real output

The repository's own comparison of low and high temperature occupancy, for 5000 evenly spaced energy levels.

Occupancy at low T (200) vs high T (800)

Both curves start at their tallest at E = 0 and decay — that never changes. What changes is the rate: at T = 200 the probability has essentially vanished by energy level 1000, while at T = 800 it's still non-negligible past 3000. Same law, different temperature, very different spread.

05 · A single vibrating degree of freedom

Harmonic oscillators, damped and undamped

Zoom into any one bond in the molecular dynamics simulation below, or any one mode of thermal vibration, and to a first approximation it behaves like a mass on a spring. The repository solves this system's equation of motion two ways: with and without friction.

i · the physics
m·x″ = −k·x  (no damping)   |   m·x″ = −k·x − b·x′  (damped)

Without damping, the restoring force −kx keeps trading energy between kinetic and potential with nothing lost — the amplitude never decays, oscillating forever at a fixed frequency. Add the −b·x′ drag term, proportional to velocity, and energy continuously bleeds out of the system: the amplitude decays exponentially while it keeps oscillating.

This is also a direct link to temperature: by the equipartition theorem, a thermal oscillator in contact with a bath at temperature T carries an average energy of ½kT per quadratic degree of freedom — the same T that set the width of the Boltzmann curve above.

iii · the real output

Both cases, solved properly with a numerical ODE integrator over 50 seconds.

No damping

A clean, constant-amplitude sine wave. Energy has nowhere to go, so the oscillation never dies down — it would keep going forever in this idealised model.

With damping (b = 0.1)

Same starting conditions, same spring — but the peaks visibly shrink each cycle. That's the −b·x′ term steadily draining energy out of the system as heat.

06 · Many oscillators, interacting

Molecular dynamics

Scale the spring-and-mass picture up to hundreds of particles, replace the spring force with a realistic interatomic potential, and you get molecular dynamics — the code integrates Newton's second law for every pair of particles, 10,000 times over.

i · the physics

Particles interact through the Lennard-Jones potential — strongly repulsive at very short range (particles can't overlap), weakly attractive a bit further out, negligible beyond that:

V(r) = 4ε[(σ/r)¹² − (σ/r)⁶]

At every step, the code sums the force from every pair of particles, then advances positions and velocities with the velocity Verlet integrator — the same idea as solving the oscillator's equation of motion above, just applied to every particle at once, with forces recomputed each step because every particle's neighbours keep moving.

The one thing this integrator is specifically built to get right: total energy conservation. Kinetic and potential energy can and do trade back and forth, but their sum should stay flat.

ii · watch it happen

The orange and green curves — kinetic and potential energy — swing around and even cross, particles constantly trading energy as they collide and separate. The blue line, total energy, barely moves at all: that flatness is the whole point of using a velocity Verlet integrator, and it's the numerical signature of a physically correct simulation.

07 · The technique this whole module runs on

Monte Carlo estimate of π

Every simulation above — Metropolis flips, random walk steps, particle collisions — leans on the same trick: replace an intractable calculation with enough random samples that the average converges to the true answer. This is that trick in its purest form.

i · the physics

Drop points uniformly at random inside a 2×2 square. A point lands inside the inscribed unit circle with probability equal to the ratio of the two areas:

P(inside circle) = π·r² / (2r)² = π/4   ⟹   π ≈ 4 × (points inside / points total)

This is the law of large numbers doing the work: no single point tells you anything, but the fraction landing inside converges to the true probability as the sample size grows — exactly the same statistical logic that lets the Ising model's Metropolis average, taken over thousands of steps, converge to the true thermal average at a given temperature.

No. of points estimated PI value actual PI value --------------------------------------------------------------------- 100 2.92000 3.14159 500 3.05600 3.14159 1000 3.14400 3.14159 5000 3.13680 3.14159 10000 3.13280 3.14159 50000 3.13792 3.14159 100000 3.14144 3.14159 200000 3.14344 3.14159 400000 3.14417 3.14159 600000 3.14247 3.14159 1000000 3.14162 3.14159

Notice it isn't monotonic — 400,000 points landed slightly closer than 600,000 did. That's expected: convergence here is statistical, not guaranteed step by step, only guaranteed in the limit.

08 · The shapes randomness takes

Probability distributions

Four distributions the code samples directly, each one already at work somewhere else in this module — or in the reaction dynamics module next door.

i · the physics

Gaussian — what you get from summing many independent random effects, by the Central Limit Theorem. It's why the 1D random walk's endpoint histogram above was already curving toward a bell shape with just fifty samples.

Poisson — the count of random, independent events in a fixed window. This is exactly the distribution behind radioactive decay counts, which shows up directly in the reaction dynamics module.

Binomial — the count of successes in a fixed number of independent yes/no trials. A row of Ising spins, each independently up or down, is a binomial variable in disguise.

Exponential — the waiting time between independent random events. This is the distribution of "time until the next decay," and it's what makes the Gillespie-style stochastic simulations elsewhere in the repository work at all.

ii · watch it happen
Live samples (n = 1000, matching the code)
sample mean—
sample variance—

Each button draws 1000 fresh random samples in the browser and rebuilds the histogram, the same way the repository's script does with numpy.

iii · the real output

All four, sampled and plotted together by the actual script.

Four distributions, 1000 samples each

Poisson and binomial are both discrete and both skewed right at these parameters (λ = 5, and n = 10, p = 0.5) — but binomial is capped at n = 10 while Poisson has no upper bound, which is why its right tail stretches further. Gaussian is the only symmetric one here. Exponential decays fastest at 0 and never has a "typical" value the way the others do — most waiting times are short, with a long thin tail of rare long ones.

Reaction Dynamics Modelling

When quantities react with each other over time.

Every model here describes a set of quantities — animal populations, molecule counts, radioactive atoms — that grow, shrink, and convert into each other according to fixed rules. Each one is solved two ways: as a smooth deterministic average, and as a jittery stochastic simulation of individual random events. Real-world analogies throughout, then the actual output from the repository.

00 · Deterministic vs stochastic 01 · Lotka–Volterra 02 · Brusselator 03 · Oregonator 04 · Radioactive decay 05 · Four-reaction model
00 · The choice every model here makes

Deterministic vs. stochastic

Every reaction network on this page gets built twice. Here's the difference between the two approaches, before any of the chemistry or ecology gets involved.

Deterministic: treat the quantities as smooth, continuous numbers and write down a differential equation for how their average changes. Solve it and you get one exact curve — the same curve every time you run it. This is accurate when the numbers involved are huge: a flask with 10²³ molecules behaves, on average, exactly like the equation predicts, because random fluctuations from any one molecule are utterly swamped by the sheer number of them.

Stochastic: treat every single event — one animal being born, one pair of molecules colliding and reacting — as a random occurrence with some probability per unit time, and simulate them one at a time (the Gillespie algorithm, used throughout this repository). Run it twice and you get two different, noisy trajectories. This is the more honest picture when the numbers involved are small.

a real-life way to feel this

Flip one coin: the outcome is completely unpredictable — that's stochastic. Flip a million coins and count the fraction landing heads: it'll be extremely close to 50%, every single time — that's the deterministic limit emerging from a huge number of random individual events. Every "deterministic" curve on this page is really that same law of large numbers, applied to molecules or animals instead of coins.

Deterministic

One smooth curve. Same result every run. Accurate for large populations. Solved with an ODE integrator (odeint / solve_ivp in the code).

Stochastic

A jittery, unique-every-time trace. Accurate for small populations. Solved event-by-event with the Gillespie algorithm.

population size N = 20
Real coins, flipped every tick — small N looks stochastic (jagged), large N looks deterministic (settles near 50%). Drag the slider.
01 · Predator and prey

Lotka–Volterra model

Two reactions, two species, one of the oldest models in mathematical biology.

the real-world picture
grass → deer → wolves

Grass is everywhere and never runs out (in this simple model, food for the prey is assumed unlimited) — so deer (Y1) breed freely and their numbers grow. Wolves (Y2) can only grow by eating deer, so more deer means more well-fed wolves. But more wolves means more deer get eaten, so the deer population crashes — and then the wolves, with less food, start starving and their numbers crash too. With fewer wolves, the deer recover, and the whole cycle repeats. That endless boom-and-bust cycle is exactly what the two reactions below produce.

the two reactions
Y1 → 2Y1   (deer reproduce, rate k1)
Y1 + Y2 → 2Y2   (a wolf eats a deer, gains offspring; rate k2)
(Y2 → ∅ is folded in as a natural wolf death rate k3)

Turn those two reactions into rate equations and you get the classic Lotka–Volterra pair:

dY1/dt = k1·Y1 − k2·Y1·Y2
dY2/dt = k2·Y1·Y2 − k3·Y2
deterministic vs stochastic, here

Deterministic (odeint)

Fractional "populations" evolving smoothly — a good approximation for a large, well-mixed ecosystem. Produces a perfectly repeating cycle every time.

Stochastic (Gillespie)

Whole-number deer and wolves, birth/predation/death firing as individual random events. Realistic for a smaller population, and the cycle amplitude visibly drifts run to run.

watch it happen
Live population
deer (Y1)—
wolves (Y2)—

Switch modes mid-run: the deterministic curve is silky-smooth; the stochastic one is jagged and never repeats the same way twice.

the real output

All four plots straight from the repository — deterministic and stochastic, each as a time series and a phase portrait.

Deterministic — population vs time

A perfectly repeating cycle: wolves (orange) peak just after deer (blue), lag behind exactly as the "eat, then breed" logic of the reaction predicts.

The same cycle, replotted as deer vs wolves instead of vs time. A closed loop means a perfectly periodic cycle that never grows or decays — the mathematical signature of this exact model.

Stochastic — population vs time

The same boom-and-bust rhythm, but ragged — and notice the swings actually grow larger over these 10 time units, purely from the accumulated randomness of individual births and deaths.

02 · A reaction that feeds itself

Brusselator model

Named for Brussels, where Prigogine and Lefever built it as the simplest possible chemical scheme that still oscillates — a minimal stand-in for real self-sustaining reactions.

the real-world picture
a fire that makes more fire

Think of a slow-burning fire fed by a steady trickle of fuel. Most of the time it just smoulders. But if it happens to catch — a bit more heat makes the fuel burn faster, which makes more heat, which burns fuel even faster — it flares up fast. Then it runs out of the fuel that had built up, and drops back to smouldering until enough fuel accumulates again. That "catches, flares, exhausts itself, repeat" rhythm is precisely what the reaction step below encodes, just with molecules instead of flames.

the four reactions
X → Y1  (rate c1, a steady input)
X2 + Y1 → Y2 + Z1  (rate c2)
2Y1 + Y2 → 3Y1  (rate c3, the self-feeding step)
Y1 → Z2  (rate c4, decay)

That third reaction is the important one: two Y1 molecules team up with a Y2 to make three Y1 — Y1 is catalysing its own production. As long as Y2 has built up, Y1 rapidly consumes it and multiplies; once Y2 runs low, Y1 stalls, decays away via the fourth reaction, and the slow build-up starts again.

deterministic vs stochastic, here

Deterministic (solve_ivp, RK45)

Thousands of "molecules" treated as continuous concentrations. Produces a clean, perfectly repeating relaxation oscillation — sharp spikes, flat troughs.

Stochastic (Gillespie)

Same reactions, whole-molecule counts, random firing order. The spikes still happen — the feedback loop is strong enough to survive the noise — but their height and timing jitter.

03 · A real oscillating reaction

Oregonator model

Unlike the Brusselator, this one models an actual, famous chemical reaction — not just its spirit.

the real-world picture
the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction

Mix a specific cocktail of chemicals in a dish and, instead of settling to a steady colour, it keeps changing — cycling between orange and colourless (or blue and red, with a different catalyst) over and over, for minutes at a stretch, with no outside interference. It looks alive. It isn't — it's a chemical feedback loop where an intermediate species inhibits its own production once it builds up too far, then relaxes and lets the cycle restart. The Oregonator (developed at the University of Oregon) is the equation set that captures this: three coupled species chasing each other in a loop, each one's rise triggering the next one's rise and eventually its own fall.

the five reactions
X1 + Y2 → Y1  (k1)
Y1 + Y2 → Z1  (k2)
X2 + Y1 → 2Y1 + Y3  (k3, autocatalytic in Y1)
2Y1 → Z2  (k4)
X3 + Y3 → Y2  (k5, closes the loop back to Y2)

Y1 makes more of itself (reaction 3) — same self-feeding trick as the Brusselator — but here Y1 also produces Y3, and Y3 eventually regenerates Y2, which is what Y1 needs to get going in the first place. Three species, chasing each other around a loop, each one setting up the next one's spike.

Y1 feeds Y2 and Y3; Y3 feeds back into Y2 (dashed) — a loop, not a one-way street.
deterministic vs stochastic, here

Deterministic (solve_ivp, RK45)

04 · The simplest reaction on this page

Radioactive decay

One species, one reaction, one direction: A → B. Simple enough to be the cleanest possible illustration of deterministic vs stochastic.

the real-world picture
an unstable atom, waiting to decay

Take a lump of a radioactive isotope — say, carbon-14. Every single atom in it is unstable, and at any moment has some small, fixed probability of decaying into nitrogen-14. Crucially, each atom's decay is a private, random event: it doesn't matter how long that particular atom has already survived, or what its neighbours are doing. With a small handful of atoms, decays happen at unpredictable moments — genuinely stochastic. But real samples hold billions of atoms, and the average behaviour of that many independent random events becomes as smooth and predictable as a clock: the familiar exponential decay curve, and the idea of a fixed "half-life."

the reaction
A → B   (rate constant k)
dA/dt = −k·A
dB/dt = +k·A

Solve that and A(t) = A₀·e^(−kt) — the single cleanest exponential in the whole repository. There's no feedback loop here, no oscillation, nothing chasing anything else — just steady, one-way decay.

deterministic vs stochastic, here

Deterministic (in the repository)

Solved with odeint as a smooth exponential — the code's actual approach, appropriate for a real sample with an enormous number of atoms.

Stochastic (added here, for comparison)

Not in the original code, but worth seeing: each atom individually "rolls the dice" every tick. With enough atoms it reproduces the same smooth curve — which is the whole point of this page.

watch it happen
atoms N = 60
Individual atoms, decaying at random
still A—
decayed to B—

Each dot is one atom — amber while it's still A, teal once it's decayed to B. No dot knows what any other dot is doing.

the real output

The repository's deterministic solution.

A(t) and B(t) — the classic decay curve

A falls away exponentially while B rises to take its place — mirror images of each other, since every atom that leaves A immediately becomes one atom of B. This is the smooth limit that the random dot-by-dot simulation on the left converges to once you turn N up high enough.

05 · Putting the pieces together

Four-reaction model

The last network in the repository, and the most self-contained: decay, a reversible pairing-up, and a one-way exit, all at once.

reading the equations backward, to find the reactions
dY1/dt = −k1·Y1 − 2k2·Y1² + 2k3·Y2
dY2/dt = k2·Y1² − k3·Y2 − k4·Y2
dY3/dt = k4·Y2

Those three equations decode into exactly three reactions:

Y1 → ∅  (k1, plain decay)
2Y1 ⇌ Y2  (k2 forward, k3 reverse — reversible pairing-up)
Y2 → Y3  (k4, one-way exit)
a real reversible pairing: NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄

Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is a real gas that constantly, reversibly pairs up into dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄) and back — a genuine textbook example of exactly the "2Y1 ⇌ Y2" step here, with its own equilibrium set by how fast each direction runs. This model adds two more realistic touches on top of that same idea: Y1 also quietly decays away on its own (first reaction), and once the paired-up Y2 forms, some of it doesn't come back — it drains away permanently into a third, final product Y3 (fourth reaction). Three simple, everyday-chemistry ideas — decay, reversible pairing, and an irreversible exit — combined into one network.

why this one is deterministic-only

The repository only builds this one as an ODE system (solve_ivp, RK45) — no Gillespie version exists for it, unlike the three networks above. Given the huge starting population (100,000 molecules of Y1), the deterministic approximation is an excellent one anyway: with that many molecules, a stochastic version would trace almost exactly the same curve, just at a much higher computational cost.

the real output

The actual repository output, starting from 100,000 molecules of Y1 and nothing else.

Y1, Y2, and Y3 vs time

Y1 (blue) collapses almost instantly as it both decays and pairs up into Y2. Y2 (orange) spikes early — briefly holding a huge share of the material as the reversible pairing equilibrates — then drains steadily into Y3 (green) through the one-way exit reaction. By t = 40, essentially everything has funnelled into Y3, which then sits flat: there's no reaction left to take it anywhere else.
